aAbout: GodsView AI is a hosted live world map: a 2D map (MapLibre GL and deck.gl) with a Cesium 3D globe, fed by OpenSky aircraft, aisstream.io ships, satellites, earthquakes, NASA fire data, weather and news. Its signature piece is the Ops Center, which merges duplicate reports of the same event from agencies like USGS, GDACS and GDELT and scores every incident from 0 to 100, with country risk ratings. A free account opens the map; Pro unlocks the full camera catalogue, the photoreal globe, alerts and flight replay.
aStrengths: GodsView AI is the operational tool: the Ops Center turns a firehose of agency reports into a scored, deduplicated incident register with country risk — something most live maps don't attempt. Add Pro alerts (emergency squawks, quakes, watch areas), flight replay, a news video wall, briefs you can export, and a lifetime pricing option, and it's the better pick for journalists and researchers who monitor the world daily from any browser — especially anyone who actually wants to watch places through cameras, which World Monitor doesn't offer at all.
bAbout: World Monitor is a free, open-source (AGPL-3.0) intelligence platform by Elie Habib that aggregates live news, markets, military movements, conflicts and infrastructure into one real-time dashboard. Its homepage, dated 26 October 2026, counts 468 news and OSINT feeds, 779 attributed providers and 59 map layer types — conflicts from ACLED and UCDP, aircraft from OpenSky, vessels from AISStream, fires from NASA FIRMS, earthquakes from USGS, and market and macro data from sources including FRED, IMF and BIS. It runs as six variants — geopolitics, tech, finance, commodity, energy and positive news — in the browser, as native desktop apps, and self-hosted from its public source code. Its official pages list no webcam feature.
bStrengths: World Monitor is the deeper analytical instrument, and the more open one: a completely free core with no signup wall, AGPL-3.0 source you can inspect or self-host, six specialised dashboard variants, 468 feeds across 59 layer types, ACLED and UCDP conflict data, chokepoint tracking, and markets and macro coverage GodsView doesn't try to match. For developers it isn't close — a documented REST API, MCP server and official SDKs, against GodsView's share links and embeds. Its Pro tier costs more, but it buys an analyst platform, not just a bigger map.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. GodsView AI is a hosted live map for watching — cameras, flights, ships and an incident register that scores what it finds, free with an account and reasonably priced on Pro. World Monitor is a free, open-source analysis dashboard — no cameras, no signup, but far deeper on conflicts, chokepoints, markets and data access, with paid tiers aimed at analysts and developers. If your question is 'what can I see happening?', open GodsView AI; if it's 'what does it all mean?', open World Monitor.

faqs.a: No — they are unrelated products from different makers. GodsView AI is a closed hosted map by founder Jijo John, built around cameras and a scored Ops Center. World Monitor is a free, open-source (AGPL-3.0) intelligence dashboard by Elie Habib. GodsView AI is also a different product from the open-source God's Eye View, a distinction GodsView states on its own site.
faqs.q: Is GodsView AI the same as World Monitor?

faqs.a: Both have real free tiers, differently shaped. World Monitor's core dashboard is free with no signup at all — every layer except Resilience. GodsView AI is free only after creating a free account, and its free tier carries ads, a 30-minute viewing pause, one AI question a day and a maximum of 2 open cameras.

Only GodsView AI. It claims a catalogue of about 229,000 public cameras in about 174 countries, with 2 open on the free tier and the full catalogue on Pro. No webcam feature appears on World Monitor's official pages. For comparison, WorldEye's directory lists 74,229 public cameras, open on its free map.
faqs.q: Which has live cameras, GodsView AI or World Monitor?

faqs.a: World Monitor, clearly. It layers ACLED and UCDP conflict data, tracks 13 strategic chokepoints, and pulls markets and macro data from FRED, IMF, BIS and Finnhub across dedicated geopolitics and finance dashboards. GodsView AI covers world events through its incident feeds and Ops Center scoring instead.
faqs.q: Which is better for conflict and markets analysis?

faqs.a: World Monitor. It documents a REST API (base api.worldmonitor.app) plus an MCP server and official SDKs, sold through its API Starter ($99.99/month) and API Business ($299.99/month) plans, with MCP also included on Pro. GodsView AI offers no public API — share links and embeddable widgets only.

GodsView AI, by a wide margin: Pro is $10.99/month, $99.99/year or $199.99 lifetime, with no free trial. World Monitor Pro is $39.99/month or $359.99/year — it buys a broader analyst platform (AI analyst, digests, MCP, widget builder), but if you mainly want the map unlocked, GodsView costs far less.

intro: GodsView AI and World Monitor both promise one screen for a chaotic world — and both are hosted sites you open in a browser — but they are built for different jobs. GodsView AI is a live map centred on moving things and cameras: flights, ships, satellites and a claimed ~229,000-camera catalogue, with an Ops Center that scores incidents 0–100. World Monitor is a free, open-source intelligence dashboard by Elie Habib: 468 news and OSINT feeds across 59 layer types — conflicts, chokepoints, markets and macro data — with no cameras at all. One more disambiguation before we start: GodsView AI is a hosted product by founder Jijo John and, by its own statement, has no affiliation with the open-source God's Eye View project.
pricingA: GodsView AI is free with a free account — with banner ads, a 30-minute live-viewing pause (reload to continue), one AI question a day and two open cameras. Pro costs $10.99/month, $99.99/year or $199.99 as a one-time lifetime plan (no free trial), and unlocks the full ~229,000-camera catalogue, the photoreal 3D globe, military aircraft, NOTAMs, alerts and flight replay.
pricingB: World Monitor's core dashboard is free at $0 with no signup — every map layer except Resilience. Pro costs $39.99/month or $359.99/year and adds the WM Analyst AI chat, a personal intelligence digest, MCP connectors and the widget builder. Above that sit Pro Business at $49.99/month ($449.99/year), API Starter at $99.99/month ($899.99/year), API Business at $299.99/month ($2,699.99/year) and custom Enterprise pricing. The source code itself is free under AGPL-3.0 if you self-host.

verdictA: Choose GodsView AI if you want a hosted monitoring map — scored incidents, alerts, flight replay and a huge claimed camera catalogue — that opens in any browser and asks nothing of your computer.
verdictB: Choose World Monitor if you want geopolitical depth for free — conflict data, chokepoints, markets and AI briefs with no signup — and especially if open source, self-hosting or API access matters to you.
verdictLine: GodsView AI watches the world: cameras, moving traffic and scored incidents behind one account. World Monitor analyses it: hundreds of feeds, conflict and market panels, free and open source. Cameras and alerts point one way; depth and openness point the other.
worldEye: WorldEye is the third shape in this comparison: like both of these it's a hosted globe that opens in the browser, but its free tier needs no signup at all — unlike GodsView's account wall — and it is built camera-first, which World Monitor doesn't attempt. Its directory lists 74,229 public cameras across 109 countries, alongside live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires. It doesn't score incidents like GodsView's Ops Center or match World Monitor's conflict and markets depth, and its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) adds an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds at well under either rival's monthly price.
